new_entities.name: High-dose inositol supplementation
new_entities.description: Pharmacologic-dose inositol supplementation, often around 18 g/day, used experimentally in obsessive-compulsive and related disorders.

new_entities.name: Obsessive-compulsive disorder severity
new_entities.description: Clinician-rated severity of obsessive-compulsive symptoms, usually measured with the Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale.

edges.effect_quant: The most optimistic direct trial remains the 1996 crossover study, where 18 g/day of inositol lowered Y-BOCS scores more than placebo in 13 patients. That early signal did not hold up in a later meta-analysis of anxiety-disorder trials, which found no statistically significant effect of inositol on obsessive-compulsive symptoms across the available randomized evidence.
edges.population: adults with obsessive-compulsive disorder or related anxiety-spectrum conditions treated with pharmacologic-dose inositol
edges.mechanism: Inositol may affect obsessive-compulsive symptoms through second-messenger and serotonergic signaling pathways that overlap with SSRI-responsive circuitry. The trouble is that mechanistic plausibility and one early positive OCD study have not translated into a stable pooled efficacy signal.
edges.summary: High-dose inositol remains a genuinely mixed OCD edge. A small early crossover trial looked promising, but broader pooled evidence has been null or inconclusive, leaving the intervention in the realm of exploratory adjunctive therapy rather than established treatment.
edges.caveats: The human OCD evidence base is tiny and old, and even the meta-analysis relies on a very small anxiety-disorder subset. This edge should not be interpreted as strong support for inositol in OCD despite the favorable signal from the original pilot study.

evidence.citation: FuxM et al 1996 Am J Psychiatry

evidence.notes: A meta-analysis of inositol for depression and anxiety disorders.
